title: Misfiring Meritocracy
author: Renn, Aaron
summary: Using the New York Times' contested list of top 30 living American songwriters as a springboard, Aaron Renn examines whether the modern credentialing system produces the elite quality its meritocratic claims promise. The bulk of the article engages a debate between historians Tanner Greer and Geoffrey Kabaservice about which model -- the Gilded Age/Progressive Era WASP establishment or the 1940-1970 postwar establishment -- offers the better template for Silicon Valley's aspiring ruling class. Both historians agree on a central point that Renn foregrounds: the legitimacy of the old establishment depended not on its members' credentials but on their willingness to subordinate class interest to national interest and make personal sacrifices for the broader good. Today's credentialed elites -- tech founders, financiers, upper-middle-class professionals -- have the credential and the position but entirely lack this ethos of public service and class sacrifice. Renn also emphasizes, via Gramsci, that durable hegemony requires the leading group to take genuine account of the governed's interests -- a condition absent from current elite formations. The article closes by noting the missing element in current accounts: the streak of self-critique within the WASP class that helped regulate its conduct.
points: The modern credentialing system has inverted the old model: elite schools once formed already-destined leaders with an ethos; now they provide credentials to those who would not otherwise reach top positions -- and the ethos is absent.

Kabaservice argues the 1940-1970 postwar establishment is the better template because it was more egalitarian, more institutionally creative, and demonstrated genuine willingness to build institutions that undermined its own dominance for the national good.

Both Greer and Kabaservice agree the establishment's core function was regulating high-stakes internal conflict while keeping participants in personal relationship -- the opposite of today's zero-sum, winner-takes-all culture wars.

Renn invokes Gramsci's point that hegemony requires economic-corporate sacrifices from the leading group -- genuine accounting for the interests of the governed -- which today's tech and finance elites flatly refuse.

The missing element in all three accounts (Greer, Kabaservice, Renn) is the WASP establishment's capacity for self-critique: an internal corrective force that helped regulate the class's conduct and gave it moral seriousness.
quotes: It used to be that prep schools and elite colleges took people who were already destined to become top leaders due to family background, and formed them with a particular ethos. Now those schools provide those who would not otherwise likely become top leaders with the credential that allows them to obtain those positions.

This illustrates the way that our present system of credentialing, filtering, and elevating people is not producing the results we would necessarily expect from a system that's supposed to be organized around skills, competence, and merit.

Kabaservice here also emphasizes what I call the 'human-social stack,' focused on making sure that techo-industrial acceleration worked well for America and Americans broadly, not just a narrow stratum of industrialists. So much focus today is on how we accelerate new technologies, build more housing or energy, etc. But the social structures and institutions in which this is embedded and deployed are of equal importance.

This ability of the establishment to make space within itself for high-stakes conflict, while regulating the conduct of that conflict, and ensuring its participants retained personal relationships and ties, was one of the establishment's core functions. In our age of no-holds-barred, zero-sum, winner-takes-all political and cultural wars, we feel keenly the lack of this establishment function today.

What made the establishment durable -- and indeed gave it legitimacy -- was less lockstep agreement on political issues than an ethos that subordinated class interest to national interest. At its heart was a compromise that involved not just the negotiated mutual absorption of two rival groups but their adjustment to a higher national creed.

The New England aristocracy allowed the 'crude but vital America' into its ranks, while the industrialists agreed to Puritan-inspired limits on their pursuit of profit at all costs. The establishment that emerged did, at its best, prove willing to incorporate talented outsiders, to adhere to an ethos of disinterested public service, to abide by norms of liberal democracy, and to build institutions that ultimately undermined its own dominance.

Undoubtedly the fact of hegemony presupposes that account be taken of the interests and the tendencies of the groups over which hegemony is to be exercised, and that a certain compromise equilibrium should be formed -- in other words, that the leading group should make sacrifices of an economic-corporate kind. [Gramsci, Prison Notebooks, cited by Renn]
This is a critical element missing from the worldview of Silicon Valley elites, Wall Street financiers, and other would-be dominant groups like 'the 9.9%' upper middle class.
